option1: Because FeeDecorator and RewardDecorator extend PaymentDecorator and need direct access to ip inside their own overridden pay() methods — a private field would be invisible to them
option2: There's no real reason — private would work identically here
option3: Because protected fields are automatically initialized to null if never set
option4: Because interfaces require all wrapped fields to be protected by default
correctOptionExplanation: Same rule seen back in class-16/17: private members of a base class are invisible to subclasses, so anything a subclass needs to touch directly must be at least protected.

questionText: FeeDecorator's constructor calls super(ip) instead of directly writing this.ip = ip. What would break if FeeDecorator tried this.ip = ip directly instead, given ip is declared in PaymentDecorator?
option1: FeeDecorator would need to redeclare its own separate ip field first
option2: It wouldn't compile as a standalone statement in the constructor unless super(ip) (or another constructor call) runs first — but more importantly, since ip is inherited, this.ip = ip inside FeeDecorator's constructor would still work fine AFTER super() runs; skipping super(ip) entirely would leave ip unset (null) unless assigned manually
option3: protected fields cannot be assigned from a subclass constructor under any circumstance
option4: this.ip and super.ip refer to completely different fields with no relationship
correctOptionExplanation: super(ip) is the cleanest way to initialize an inherited field; skipping it entirely (with no other assignment) would leave ip null.

questionText: PaymentDecorator implements IPayment but never overrides pay() itself. Given pay() is abstract in IPayment, why doesn't PaymentDecorator fail to compile despite not providing a body for it?
option1: IPayment.pay() must be declared with a default body for this to work
option2: PaymentDecorator secretly does implement pay(), it's just hidden by the abstract keyword
option3: PaymentDecorator is itself declared abstract, which allows a class to implement an interface while still leaving some of its methods unimplemented — the obligation to provide a body passes down to whichever concrete subclass eventually extends it
option4: Java automatically supplies an empty default body for any unimplemented interface method
correctOptionExplanation: Abstract classes can defer implementing interface methods to their own subclasses — this is exactly how PaymentDecorator stays valid without a pay() body.

option1: "deducting fee", then "adding reward points", then "paying using UPI"
option2: "paying using UPI", then "adding reward points", then "deducting fee"
option3: "adding reward points", then "deducting fee", then "paying using UPI"
option4: "paying using UPI", then "deducting fee", then "adding reward points"
correctOptionExplanation: Tracing inside-out: UPI.pay() runs first (innermost), then FeeDecorator's own line, then RewardDecorator's own line as the call unwinds back outward.

questionText: Now suppose FeeDecorator.pay() is changed to print "deducting fee" BEFORE calling ip.pay(), while RewardDecorator.pay() stays unchanged (calls ip.pay() first, then prints "adding reward points"). For the same RewardDecorator(FeeDecorator(UPI())) construction, what changes in the output?
option1: "deducting fee" now prints before "paying using UPI", since FeeDecorator's own logic runs before it delegates to UPI — the overall order becomes: "deducting fee", "paying using UPI", "adding reward points"
option2: This causes a compile error since decorators must always call ip.pay() first
option3: Nothing changes — decorator ordering in output is fixed regardless of where each decorator places its own logic relative to ip.pay()
option4: "adding reward points" would now print first instead
correctOptionExplanation: Where a decorator places its own logic relative to the delegated call is entirely up to that decorator's implementation, and directly determines output order.

questionText: A coffee shop app has Beverage interface with double cost() and String getDescription(). Espresso implements Beverage returns a base cost. You want to support "add milk" and "add caramel" as optional add-ons, in any combination, without writing EspressoWithMilk, EspressoWithCaramel, EspressoWithMilkAndCaramel as separate classes. What's the decorator-based fix?
option1: Create one Beverage subclass per combination, since that's the only way to support "any combination"
option2: BeverageDecorator implements Beverage (holding a Beverage field), with MilkDecorator and CaramelDecorator each extending it, overriding cost() to add their own charge on top of the wrapped beverage's cost, and getDescription() to append their own label — stacked via constructor nesting, same as the payment example
option3: Add a boolean hasMilk and boolean hasCaramel field directly to Espresso, with cost() branching on both flags internally
option4: Make Beverage an abstract class with hasMilk() and hasCaramel() as required overrides for every implementer
correctOptionExplanation: Same shape as the payment decorators — a shared abstract base plus concrete add-on decorators stacked freely at construction time.

option1: beverage.cost() is required syntax whenever a field is typed as an interface
option2: This is only necessary if Espresso has multiple constructors
option3: Because beverage could be a plain Espresso, or it could be another decorator (like a CaramelDecorator wrapping an Espresso) — calling beverage.cost() polymorphically lets MilkDecorator work correctly no matter what it's actually wrapping, without ever needing to know
option4: Hardcoding the price would actually work identically and is just a style preference
correctOptionExplanation: Polymorphic delegation is what makes stacking work at all — the decorator never needs to know or care what's really underneath it.

questionText: A junior dev suggests skipping decorators entirely and just adding boolean hasMilk, boolean hasCaramel, boolean hasWhippedCream fields directly onto Espresso, with cost() summing up whichever flags are true. Functionally this can produce the same prices. What does it lose compared to the decorator version?
option1: The flag-based version would actually be more type-safe than decorators
option2: Nothing is lost — both approaches are equally extensible
option3: The flag-based version supports unlimited add-ons while decorators cap out at two
option4: Every new add-on requires editing Espresso's own source code to add another flag and another line in cost()'s calculation — the decorator version lets you add a WhippedCreamDecorator as a brand-new class with zero changes to Espresso, MilkDecorator, or CaramelDecorator
correctOptionExplanation: Same OCP violation seen with Simple Factory's if-else — every extension forces an edit to existing source, unlike the additive decorator approach.

questionText: If CaramelDecorator needs to know the SIZE of the drink (small/medium/large) to charge a different caramel price, but Beverage.cost() takes no parameters at all, what real constraint does this expose about decorators?
option1: A decorator can only use information available through the interface it implements (or fields it's given at construction) — if cost()'s signature carries no size information, the decorator can't magically know it unless the interface is widened or the decorator is given the size separately at construction
option2: This is impossible to solve — decorators cannot use any external information beyond what they wrap
option3: Beverage.cost() needs to be made static to fix this
option4: Decorators automatically have access to every field on whatever object they wrap, regardless of interface
correctOptionExplanation: Same signature-carries-everything limitation seen with Observer's notifyUser(String) not knowing which channel sent it — the interface's shape bounds what a decorator can know.

questionText: A text-formatting library has Text interface with String render(). PlainText implements Text just returns raw text. You want BoldDecorator and ItalicDecorator that wrap any Text and add markup. If you construct new BoldDecorator(new ItalicDecorator(new PlainText("hello"))), and BoldDecorator.render() wraps its inner text.render() output in **...**, while ItalicDecorator.render() wraps its inner output in *...*, what's the final rendered string?
option1: "hello" unchanged, since decorators only affect cost()-style numeric methods, not strings
option2: The correct trace is: PlainText.render() returns "hello", ItalicDecorator wraps it to "*hello*", then BoldDecorator wraps that to "**" + "*hello*" + "**", producing "***hello***"
option3: "*hello*" only — BoldDecorator is ignored since ItalicDecorator already returned a value
option4: The program throws a runtime exception since two decorators can't wrap the same string twice
correctOptionExplanation: Decorators work identically whether the return type is a number or a string — each layer wraps whatever the inner call produced.

questionText: In the text-formatting example, what would change if you constructed new ItalicDecorator(new BoldDecorator(new PlainText("hello"))) instead — same two decorators, reversed order?
option1: It's impossible to reverse decorator order once written
option2: The output would be completely empty
option3: The final string is still visually similar (***hello***) since the markers stack either way here, but the actual markup layering order differs internally — bold gets applied first, then italic wraps around it, which matters if the rendering rules for combined markup ever differ by nesting order
option4: ItalicDecorator cannot wrap BoldDecorator since both extend the same base class
correctOptionExplanation: Nesting order always matters structurally, even when two particular decorators happen to produce visually similar output for this specific example.

questionText: Going back to the strategy-mixing idea discussed for payments: FeeDecorator holds both an IPayment ip (from PaymentDecorator) AND a FeeStrategy feeStrategy (injected separately). Which design principle does injecting feeStrategy via the constructor, rather than hardcoding fee logic inside FeeDecorator.pay(), actually demonstrate?
option1: Observer — because FeeDecorator notifies the strategy of every payment
option2: This has no formal name; it's just convenient shorthand
option3: Singleton — because only one FeeStrategy object should ever exist
option4: Dependency Injection combined with Strategy — FeeDecorator depends on the FeeStrategy abstraction rather than a concrete calculation, so the actual fee logic can vary (CardFeeStrategy vs UpiFeeStrategy) without changing FeeDecorator's own source code
correctOptionExplanation: Constructor-injecting a behavior-defining interface, rather than hardcoding a specific calculation, is exactly the Strategy pattern's shape.

option1: No — since both CardFeeStrategy and UpiFeeStrategy implement the same FeeStrategy interface, this compiles fine; the mismatch is a logical/business error (wrong fee rule applied to Card), not a type error the compiler can catch
option2: Yes — this throws a ClassCastException immediately
option3: No, and there's no real risk here since fee calculation logic is identical across strategies anyway
option4: Yes — Java enforces that a Card object can only be paired with a CardFeeStrategy at compile time
correctOptionExplanation: The type system only checks that the strategy satisfies the interface, not that it's the semantically correct one for the paired payment type.

questionText: Given the previous question's finding — that mismatched payment/strategy pairs compile fine but are logically wrong — what's a reasonable way to reduce (not eliminate) this risk without abandoning the Strategy-injection design?
option1: There's no reasonable fix; Strategy injection should be abandoned entirely for this use case
option2: A factory method (e.g. PaymentFactory.createCardPaymentWithFee()) that always constructs the correct Card + CardFeeStrategy pairing internally, so calling code never manually mismatches them — while still allowing direct construction for flexibility when genuinely needed
option3: Force Card to extend CardFeeStrategy directly so mismatches become impossible
option4: Make FeeStrategy a single class with an if-else on payment type internally, removing the need for separate strategy classes
correctOptionExplanation: A factory that pairs the correct concrete types together is a common way to keep flexible constructors while reducing the chance of accidental mismatches.

questionText: A gift-wrapping e-commerce feature: Product interface has double getPrice(). You want GiftWrapDecorator (adds a flat wrapping fee) and PersonalizedNoteDecorator (adds a smaller flat fee) — both being purely additive dollar amounts with no type-specific variation needed. Does this scenario actually need Strategy mixed in, or is plain Decorator enough?
option1: This scenario is impossible to solve with Decorator, only Strategy can handle add-on pricing
option2: It requires both Decorator and Strategy no matter what, since Strategy is mandatory in any Decorator use case
option3: Plain Decorator is enough here — since neither wrapping fee nor note fee varies by product type, there's no second axis of variation to justify adding Strategy; introducing it would be unnecessary complexity for a problem that doesn't exist yet
option4: Strategy is always required whenever more than one decorator exists
correctOptionExplanation: Strategy should only be added when there's genuine type-specific variation to handle — not by default on every decorator.

questionText: This connects to a bigger point: Strategy should only be layered into Decorator when there's a genuine second axis of variation (like fee logic differing by payment type). What's the risk of reflexively adding Strategy to every decorator "just in case," even when nothing currently varies by type?
option1: There's no risk — more abstraction is always strictly better regardless of whether it's currently needed
option2: It would make the code impossible to unit test
option3: It would cause a runtime performance penalty in every case
option4: It adds real complexity (extra interfaces, extra classes, extra constructor parameters) for a dimension of variation that doesn't exist yet, making the code harder to read and reason about without providing any actual current benefit — premature generalization
correctOptionExplanation: Adding abstraction ahead of an actual need is a real cost, not a free safety margin — this is the premature-generalization trap.

questionText: A car customization app has Vehicle interface with double getPrice(). SedanBase implements Vehicle returns a base price. SunroofDecorator and LeatherSeatsDecorator each add their own flat cost. If a dealership later wants sunroof pricing to differ by car MODEL (sedan vs SUV) while leather seat pricing stays flat regardless of model, how would you apply what was just discussed?
option1: Only SunroofDecorator needs a SunroofPricingStrategy injected (since only its logic varies by model) — LeatherSeatsDecorator can stay a plain decorator with hardcoded flat pricing, since nothing about its behavior varies by an external factor
option2: This requires switching the whole design to Factory Method instead of Decorator
option3: Both decorators must get a strategy injected, since consistency across all decorators is required
option4: Neither decorator can use Strategy since Vehicle.getPrice() takes no parameters
correctOptionExplanation: Strategy is applied selectively, only where a real second axis of variation actually exists — not uniformly across every decorator in the system.

questionText: Circle back to something clarified earlier: Adapter and Decorator both wrap an object and implement a shared interface. Given a PaymentDecorator implements IPayment and (hypothetically) a LegacyCashAdapter implements IPayment both sitting in your codebase, could you validly do new FeeDecorator(new LegacyCashAdapter(new OldCashRegister()))?
option1: No — this would require LegacyCashAdapter and FeeDecorator to be in the same class hierarchy
option2: Yes — since LegacyCashAdapter satisfies IPayment (that's its whole job), FeeDecorator's constructor (which just needs an IPayment) doesn't care whether what it's wrapping is a plain payment class, another decorator, or an adapter bridging something entirely incompatible
option3: Yes, but only if OldCashRegister also implements IPayment directly
option4: No — Adapter-produced objects can never be passed into a Decorator's constructor
correctOptionExplanation: Because both patterns are built around the same target-interface shape, objects produced by one can be freely composed with the other.

questionText: Given the previous question's answer, what does this reveal about why both Adapter and Decorator are built around "implement the target interface, hold the wrapped object via composition"?
option1: It only works because IPayment has exactly one method
option2: It's a coincidence with no real design significance
option3: That shared shape is exactly what makes them freely composable with each other — any object satisfying IPayment (whether original, decorated, or adapted) can be treated identically by any code (including other decorators) expecting IPayment, regardless of how many layers of translation or added behavior sit underneath
option4: It means Adapter and Decorator are actually the same pattern despite different names
correctOptionExplanation: Consistent target-interface-plus-composition is precisely what lets independently-written wrapping classes interoperate seamlessly.

questionText: A notification system has INotifier interface with void notifyUser(String msg). EmailNotifier and SMSNotifier implement it directly. You want to add "retry on failure" and "log every attempt" as optional wrap-around behaviors, usable on either notifier, in any combination. Sketch the decorator class names and what each would need to hold.
option1: Add boolean shouldRetry and boolean shouldLog fields directly to INotifier interface itself
option2: RetryDecorator and LoggingDecorator should each directly extend EmailNotifier, since that's the most common notifier type
option3: RetryEmailNotifier, RetrySMSNotifier, LoggingEmailNotifier, LoggingSMSNotifier, LoggingRetryEmailNotifier, LoggingRetrySMSNotifier — one class per combination
option4: NotifierDecorator implements INotifier (abstract, holds a protected INotifier notifier field, constructor takes an INotifier), with RetryDecorator and LoggingDecorator each extending it and overriding notifyUser() to add their own behavior around a call to notifier.notifyUser(msg)
correctOptionExplanation: Same shared-base-plus-concrete-decorators shape as every other example — this is the general template for the pattern regardless of domain.

questionText: In the notifier example, if RetryDecorator.notifyUser() calls notifier.notifyUser(msg) inside a loop (retrying up to 3 times if an exception is thrown), and this RetryDecorator is wrapped by a LoggingDecorator on the outside, how many times does LoggingDecorator's own logging code run per single top-level notifyUser() call?
option1: Just once overall — LoggingDecorator.notifyUser() is only invoked one time by the caller; it calls notifier.notifyUser(msg) once (which happens to be the RetryDecorator, whose own internal loop retries 3 times, but that looping is entirely inside RetryDecorator's single call, invisible to LoggingDecorator)
option2: LoggingDecorator and RetryDecorator cannot be combined since one contains a loop
option3: Three times, since LoggingDecorator wraps RetryDecorator and inherits its retry count automatically
option4: It depends on which decorator was constructed first, not which is outermost
correctOptionExplanation: Whatever happens inside one decorator's method body (including internal loops) is entirely opaque to whichever decorator wraps it — only the single call boundary is visible outward.

questionText: This raises a subtle design question: should RetryDecorator be the OUTER layer (wrapping LoggingDecorator) instead, so each individual retry attempt gets logged separately? What determines which ordering is "correct"?
option1: LoggingDecorator must always be outermost by definition of the pattern
option2: There's no universally correct ordering — it depends entirely on what behavior you actually want (log only the final outcome vs. log every retry attempt); the decorator pattern gives you the flexibility to choose either by nesting order, but doesn't dictate which is right
option3: The compiler enforces a specific required ordering based on class declaration order
option4: RetryDecorator must always be innermost by definition of the pattern
correctOptionExplanation: Ordering is a design decision left entirely to whoever constructs the chain, based on the actual behavior desired.

questionText: A test wants to verify that FeeDecorator(new Card(), someStrategy).pay() calls someStrategy.deductFee() exactly once. What makes this easy to test, given FeeStrategy is injected via the constructor rather than hardcoded?
option1: Testing decorators requires a completely different testing approach than testing plain classes
option2: FeeDecorator cannot be tested in isolation since it depends on IPayment
option3: You can inject a fake/test FeeStrategy implementation that just records whether deductFee() was called, construct FeeDecorator with it, call pay(), and assert on the fake — the same testability benefit seen with ISubscriber test doubles and constructor-injected dependencies throughout the course
option4: You would need to modify FeeStrategy's real implementations to add test-only code
correctOptionExplanation: Constructor-injected dependencies are swappable with test doubles regardless of which pattern introduced them — same benefit as always.

questionText: If PaymentDecorator's constructor didn't exist at all, and instead FeeDecorator and RewardDecorator each independently declared their own private IPayment ip field and their own constructor logic (no shared abstract base class), what would be lost structurally, even though the behavior might work identically?
option1: This is strictly better, since it removes unnecessary inheritance
option2: Decorators without a shared base class cannot be stacked
option3: The code literally would not compile without a shared abstract base class
option4: The guarantee that every decorator is substitutable wherever IPayment is expected would still hold (since each still implements IPayment directly), but the shared "holds an IPayment, exists to wrap one" structure would need to be duplicated in every decorator instead of being defined once — more repeated boilerplate, no shared enforcement point
correctOptionExplanation: The shared abstract base isn't strictly required for the pattern to function, but it centralizes common structure instead of duplicating it across every decorator.

questionText: An insurance quoting app has IPolicy interface with double getPremium(). AutoPolicy and HomePolicy implement it directly. RoadsideAssistanceDecorator adds a flat premium increase and only makes sense wrapping an AutoPolicy, never a HomePolicy. How would you enforce that RoadsideAssistanceDecorator can only wrap auto policies specifically, given its constructor is typed to accept IPolicy generically?
option1: Type the constructor parameter as AutoPolicy instead of the broader IPolicy — narrowing the accepted type at compile time trades away the ability to wrap other decorators (since a decorator wrapping an AutoPolicy isn't itself an AutoPolicy), a real tradeoff worth being aware of when a decorator is domain-specific rather than universal
option2: Add a runtime instanceof check inside the constructor that throws if the wrong type is passed, which is the only possible solution
option3: This cannot be enforced at all — any decorator must always accept the full IPolicy interface
option4: Make IPolicy require a getPolicyType() method that every decorator must check manually before allowing construction
correctOptionExplanation: Narrowing the constructor's parameter type is a real, simple compile-time enforcement option — with a real cost attached.

questionText: Given the previous question's tradeoff — narrowing RoadsideAssistanceDecorator's constructor to accept only AutoPolicy — what capability does this specifically sacrifice compared to keeping it typed as IPolicy?
option1: It would break AutoPolicy.getPremium() itself
option2: You could no longer stack another decorator underneath it (e.g. wrapping some OtherAutoDecorator first, then RoadsideAssistanceDecorator on top), since a decorator that itself only implements IPolicy (not AutoPolicy specifically) wouldn't satisfy the narrowed constructor
option3: It would prevent AutoPolicy from ever being decorated by anything else afterward
option4: Nothing is sacrificed — narrowing the type has zero functional consequences
correctOptionExplanation: Narrowing the accepted type trades away composability with other decorators for tighter compile-time guarantees — a genuine tradeoff, not a free win.

questionText: Zooming out across payment, coffee, text, notifier, and insurance examples — in every single one, the concrete decorators (FeeDecorator, MilkDecorator, BoldDecorator, RetryDecorator, RoadsideAssistanceDecorator) each did the same two things inside their overridden method. What are those two things?
option1: Log the call and then throw an exception if the wrapped object is null
option2: Construct a brand-new object of the wrapped type and discard the original
option3: Delegate to the wrapped object's corresponding method (so whatever's underneath still runs), and add their own additional behavior/value on top — the delegation is mandatory for correctness, the "add-on" logic is the actual point of that specific decorator existing
option4: Convert the wrapped object's return type into a different type entirely
correctOptionExplanation: This is the universal shape of every decorator regardless of domain: delegate plus add — nothing more is required by the pattern.

questionText: If a decorator's overridden method FORGETS to call the wrapped object's corresponding method at all (e.g. FeeDecorator.pay() only prints "deducting fee" but never calls ip.pay()), what breaks, concretely?
option1: It would cause a StackOverflowError due to infinite recursion
option2: Nothing breaks — the wrapped object's method runs automatically regardless
option3: This causes an immediate compile-time error, since forgetting to call the wrapped method is statically checked by Java
option4: The underlying payment (Card, UPI, or whatever's wrapped) never actually executes — the whole chain beneath that decorator is silently skipped, even though the decorator itself runs without any error or exception
correctOptionExplanation: Nothing in the type system enforces that a decorator actually delegates — forgetting the call is a silent logic bug, not a compile error.

questionText: Compare this "forgot to delegate" bug in decorators to something already found in class-21 Observer, where YouTubeChannel.uploadVideo() forgetting to call notifySubscribers() silently broke notification without any compile error. What's the common theme between both bugs?
option1: Both patterns rely on the programmer remembering to make an internal call (delegate to the wrapped object, or notify subscribers) that nothing in the type system enforces — the compiler happily accepts code that's structurally correct but behaviorally broken, in both cases
option2: Both bugs are actually impossible in real Java code
option3: These are two completely unrelated bug categories with nothing in common
option4: Both bugs only occur when multithreading is involved
correctOptionExplanation: Both Decorator and Observer share the same class of silent-logic-bug risk: a forgotten call that the compiler cannot catch.

questionText: Tie the whole class together: a plain payment can be wrapped by any number of decorators in any order to add optional behavior, each decorator can additionally receive an injected strategy when its added behavior needs to vary by underlying type, and the entire chain stays fully interchangeable because everything ultimately satisfies the same target interface. What's the one sentence that captures why this combination (Decorator plus optional Strategy) avoids the class-explosion problem seen earlier with Simple Factory's if-else and the naive 6-class payment combo count?
option1: Because Strategy replaces Decorator entirely once more than one functionality is needed
option2: Because "which functionalities are layered on" (handled by stacking decorators) and "how a given functionality behaves for a given type" (handled by injected strategies) are treated as two independent, separately extensible axes, rather than being multiplied together into one combined class per possible combination
option3: Because Decorator and Strategy both eliminate the need for interfaces entirely
option4: Because every payment type only ever needs exactly one decorator in practice
correctOptionExplanation: This is the core payoff tying the whole session together: treating orthogonal concerns as independent axes keeps growth additive instead of multiplicative.
